Yamaha MODX

The MODX8+: the basics, using it as an audio interface, playing the site’s band on it (routing, timing, a kit per style), percussion auditions on its kits, and a whole-band A/B of site and MODX sounds.

The Yamaha MODX is a synthesizer keyboard. It has pianos, organs, strings, synths and drum kits built in. It can also be a sound card for the computer. Plug in one USB cable, and the computer can record the MODX and play sound back through it. You don’t need a separate audio interface.

The parts you’ll use

Part What it’s for
Touch screen Choose sounds (a sound is called a Performance), change settings
Super Knob (the big knob) Changes several settings at once. Turn it while you play to change the sound
Scene buttons Up to 8 saved versions of the current sound. Press one to switch
CATEGORY SEARCH Find a sound by type: Piano, Keyboard, Organ, Strings, Synth Lead, Drum…
[EXIT] Goes back one screen. Press it again and again to get home
Back panel: OUTPUT L/MONO, R Two 1/4” jacks to the mixer or speakers. Use only L for mono
Back panel: A/D INPUT Plug in a mic or guitar here to send it through the MODX
Back panel: USB TO HOST USB cable to the computer, for MIDI and audio
PHONES Headphones. Turn the master volume down before you put them on

Find a sound

  1. Press [CATEGORY SEARCH].
  2. Touch a category (for example Piano), then touch a sound in the list.
  3. Play. Turn the Super Knob to hear how the sound changes.
  4. Press [EXIT] when you’re done.

You don’t need to save to play a sound. Save only if you change one and want to keep it.

Using the MODX as an audio interface

This is the easiest way to record a keyboard part. One USB cable carries everything: the notes you play (MIDI), the sound of the MODX (audio into the computer), and the computer’s sound (audio back out of the MODX’s outputs and headphones).

Setup

  1. Connect USB TO HOST on the MODX to the computer with a USB cable (USB-A to USB-B).
  2. Turn the MODX on.
  3. On the computer, open your DAW’s audio settings:
    • Input device: Yamaha MODX
    • Output device: Yamaha MODX
    • Sample rate: 44.1 kHz
  4. Make an audio track. Set its input to the first stereo pair (1–2). Arm it and press record.
  5. Plug headphones into the MODX, or run its outputs to the mixer. You hear the computer and the keyboard together, from one place.

That’s all. No extra boxes, no extra cables, no mic stand.

Why it’s easy

  • One cable. A normal setup needs a keyboard, an audio interface, two audio cables and a USB cable. The MODX does all of it.
  • Clean sound. The audio stays digital from the MODX into the computer. Nothing to hum, no gain knob to set too high or too low.
  • One place to listen. The computer’s playback comes out of the MODX’s headphone jack, so you hear the backing track and your playing together, with no lag.
  • Mic or guitar too. Plug a mic or guitar into A/D INPUT and it goes to the computer over the same USB cable.

Things to check if it doesn’t work

Problem Try
The computer doesn’t list “Yamaha MODX” Use a different USB cable (some only charge). Plug straight into the computer, not a hub
Windows: no MODX audio device Install the Yamaha Steinberg USB Driver from Yamaha’s website
You hear yourself twice, a little late Turn off input monitoring on the DAW track. You already hear the MODX directly
No sound from the computer Check the DAW’s output device is the MODX, and the MODX master volume is up
Recording is silent Check the track’s input is 1–2 and the track is armed
Note

Unverified: Yamaha community forums disagree on whether a Mac needs the Yamaha driver or works without one, and on the exact number of USB audio channels (often quoted as 10 out to the computer and 4 back, at 44.1 kHz). Check the MODX Owner’s Manual before relying on these.

Play the site’s band on it

The band section below sends the Backing Track band’s notes to the MODX, so its bass, keys, guitar or drums play on the board instead of in the browser. It compares each sound side by side so you can pick which instruments to send. If the computer’s sound also comes out of the MODX (set the computer’s output to the MODX), both come out of the same speakers, and the timing is easier to line up.

Play the band on the MODX

Send the band’s notes to a Yamaha MODX over USB instead of playing the site’s own samples, one instrument at a time. Works in Chrome or Edge (Web MIDI). Nothing changes for anyone without a MODX: until you switch it on here, every page sounds as before. To audition the board’s congas, timbales and brushes, see the percussion auditions below.

Connect

Not connected

Plug the MODX in by USB and switch it on first. The browser asks once whether this site may use MIDI. With the box ticked, every Backing Track, lesson and tool that uses the band connects by itself and sends the instruments ticked under Routing to the MODX.

Site only
Box unticked. The site's samples, as before.
Sound module
Box ticked, some instruments routed. Those play on the MODX; the rest stay on the site.
Play along
Sound module, with Local Control on (the board's default): you play the MODX keys over the band.

The Site Band Performance

Make this once on the board and save it in a User slot. Each Part listens on its own channel, so the site can play several instruments at once without touching the board again.

Part Channel Put on it Site instruments
1 1 Upright bass bass (upright)
2 2 Wurlitzer electric piano Wurlitzer
3 3 Organ with rotary speaker tonewheel organ
4 4 Clean electric guitar electric guitar (clean)
5 5 Distorted electric guitar electric guitar (distorted)
7 7 Grand piano piano
8 8 Rhodes electric piano Rhodes
9 9 Pop Latin Kit congas, bongos
10 10 Electric bass bass (electric)
11 11 Steel-string acoustic guitar acoustic guitar (steel)
12 12 Brush Kit drums: brush grooves, and every brush stroke
13 13 BeechwoodSnare Kit drums: jazz time, Latin, blues shuffles
14 14 Rock Stereo Kit 1 drums: rock, half-time, train beat
15 15 Dry Standard Kit drums: pop, ballads, dance, Motown, folk
16 16 R&B Kit 1 drums: funk, reggaeton

Five drum kits, because one kit made some styles sound wrong. Which groove goes to which kit is set under Drum maps. On R&B Kit 1 the tom keys play 808-style kicks (Data List), so tom fills in funk sound odd.

Then, in Utility → Settings → MIDI, check that the MODX receives Bank Select and Program Change, so the button below can call the Performance up. Bank and number: in the Performance list, the User bank is shown with the number of each slot. The defaults below (MSB 63, LSB 32, program 0 = User 1, first slot) are from memory of Yamaha's MIDI tables and not yet checked on the board.

Timing

The computer's speakers and the MODX's are late by different amounts. Press Start: the site plays a stick click and the MODX a rim click at the same time. Move the slider until you hear one click instead of two. Use the speakers or headphones you'll play with.

More than zero holds the MODX back; less than zero sends it earlier (only as far as the site's own delay allows).

Compare

Each row plays the same phrase twice, the site and then the MODX (with the Site Band Performance loaded), so you can pick the better one. Your choices are kept. Route the winners sends every instrument where the MODX won to the board.

Routing

Which instruments go to the MODX, and on which channel. Instruments sharing a channel share a Part.

Shift moves an instrument's notes on the way to the MODX: 12 = an octave up, −12 = an octave down. Use it when a MODX voice sounds an octave off from the site (▶ both plays the site's phrase and then the MODX's). Velocity spreads the band's soft-to-loud over that range of MIDI velocities: 1–127 sends what the band plays; raising the low number (say 40–120) keeps a piano or Rhodes out of its dullest, softest layers. Before blaming a voice, check on the board: Utility → Settings → MIDI, MIDI I/O Mode = Multi (else one channel plays every keyboard Part); Arp Master and each Part's arpeggio and motion sequencer off; no Note Shift or Note Limit left on a Part; and no Mega Voices — the Reference Manual says they "have a very complex structure with many different layers that are not suitable for playing manually" and should be played only by their own arpeggios.

The pitch-bend range must match the Part's (2 is the usual default) or slides land on the wrong note. The rotary speed CC is what the organ's slow/fast switch sends: 1 (the mod wheel) is a guess, so check which control your organ Performance uses for it.

Drum maps

Which MODX key each drum is on. The drum keys are the General MIDI layout, which all five kits follow (checked against the Data List); the hand drums are the Pop Latin Kit's keys. Press ▶ to hear one on the MODX and change the number if it's the wrong drum.

Which kit each groove plays on: five Parts, one kit each. A groove not listed plays on the jazz kit.

Percussion auditions

Loops written for four MODX+ drum kits, sent straight to the board over USB. Use them to hear the congas, bongos, timbales, bells and brushes, and mark the ones you’d use with ☆. Works in Chrome or Edge (Web MIDI). The key maps come from Yamaha’s MODX6+/7+/8+ Data List (Drum Kit Assign List); each loop says what was checked against a source (listed under Works Cited) and what is still the site’s own guess.

Connect

Set up a Performance with the kits on these channels (change the numbers if yours differ). Press Esc to stop. The board's own offset from Timing, in the band section applies here too.

Your picks

Latin percussion (Pop Latin Kit)

Brushes (Real Brushes, Jazz Brushes, Brush Kit)

Every brush loop uses keys that mean the same thing on all three kits, so ⇄ Take turns plays it on each kit in turn (two bars each) and you can hear which you like.

Test slots (rock, pop, R&B, hip-hop)

The patterns below play on whichever kits you put in four spare Parts. Load a kit into each Part on the MODX, then choose the same kit here so the names and the ☆ marks match. ⇄ Take turns plays a pattern on all four, two bars each. Every kit listed keeps the General MIDI layout on the keys these patterns use (kick C1, snare D1, hats F#1/A#1, toms F1–D2, crash C#2, ride D#2), checked against the Data List; the grids show the drum's role, the kit walk its sample names.

Band A/B: site and MODX

Each example below is the Backing Track band in one style. Press ▶ Play, then flip Site and MODX while it plays (or press m), or tick Switch every … bars to hear them take turns. Mark which sounds better under each one; the tally is at the top. The MODX plays each instrument on its Part of the Site Band Performance and the drums on the kit for that style (set on the band section above); an instrument with no Part stays on the site.

Connect and switch

Not connected

The automatic switch times bars from the tempo, not from the band itself, so it can land a little off the barline. Set the MODX's timing offset on the MODX page first, or the two will not line up.

So far:

Swing

Walking upright bass, piano, ride time on the jazz kit (BeechwoodSnare).

Jazz ballad

Bass in two, piano pads; the drums on the jazz kit.

Bossa nova

Cross-stick bossa on the jazz kit, nylon or jazz guitar on the site, piano.

Son montuno

The clave groove on the jazz kit and the tumbao on the Pop Latin Kit’s congas (channel 9).

Jump blues

Boogie bass and a shuffle on the jazz kit.

Straight-eighth rock

Rock Stereo Kit 1 (channel 14), electric bass.

Rock, distorted guitar

The same with the distorted guitar comping (channel 5).

Acoustic strum

Steel-string guitar (channel 11), the pop kit (Dry Standard, channel 15).

Piano ballad

Piano (channel 7) and the pop kit.

Motown / soul

Snare on every beat on the pop kit, electric bass.

Soul with organ

The Motown groove with the tonewheel organ comping (channel 3; the MODX’s rotary speed on the CC set on the MODX page).

Dance pop

Four on the floor on the pop kit.

Dance pop on Rhodes

The same with the Rhodes comping (channel 8).

Reggaeton

Dembow on the R&B kit (channel 16).

Folk carol (brushes)

Brushes on the Brush Kit (channel 12).

Funk on Wurlitzer

A Wurlitzer comping (channel 2) over the soul band; switch the groove to Funk below to hear the R&B kit.

For the orchestra (sixteen Parts for the full scores, set up for later): MODX Orchestra.

Manuals

  • Yamaha, MODX+ Owner’s Manual, Reference Manual and Data List: on Yamaha’s website under Support → Manuals (copies in the teacher’s ~/Documents/Manuals).

Works Cited

Absil, Frans. “Band Latin.” www.fransabsil.nl/archpdf/bandlatn.pdf. Forward and reversed (2-3) cáscara side by side.

“Beating the Bongos.” Dummies, Wiley. www.dummies.com/article/academics-the-arts/music/instruments/drums/beating-the-bongos-199618/. Martillo: slaps on the small drum, the open tone on the large drum, soft left-hand tones.

“Bell pattern.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_pattern. The 12/8 standard pattern: 1, 1a, 2&, 2a, 3&, 4, 4a.

“Benny Benjamin.” Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, 2003. rockhall.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Benny_Benjamin_2003.pdf. His constant quarter-note snare (seen in search excerpt).

“Bernard Purdie.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Purdie. The Purdie shuffle: triplets against a half-time backbeat, ghost notes on the snare.

“Bongo Patterns.” www.lx.iriss.org.uk/read/bongo-patterns.html. Martillo: eight strokes, accents on 1, 3 and 4, beat 4 on the hembra (seen in search excerpt only; page refused direct reading).

“Boom bap.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boom_bap. Kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, highly swung programming on the MPC and SP-1200.

“Brushes.” BYU Percussion, Brigham Young University. percussion.byu.edu/brushes. Swing: right hand swings, left stirs, the hands trade places on 2 and 4; ballads: both hands stir in opposite directions.

“Cascara Rhythms.” Salsa Forums. www.salsaforums.com/threads/cascara-rhythms.26232/. The 3-2 and 2-3 cáscara counts used here (a member’s transcription).

“Cascara.” Soundbrenner. www.soundbrenner.com/blogs/articles/cascara. Cáscara follows the clave’s direction; its printed grid differs from the one used here.

“Disco.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco. Four-on-the-floor bass drum, ‘an open hissing hi-hat on the off-beat’.

“Drum beat.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_beat. Straight rock groove (kick and snare on the beats, hats on the eighths); half-time (snare on 3, hats in quarters); the delayed backbeat of funk.

“Four on the floor (music).” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_on_the_floor_(music). The bass drum on every beat; disco and dance music.

“Groove: How J Dilla Changed Rhythm.” The Pudding, June 2023. pudding.cool/2023/06/groove/. Straight, swung and shifted parts at once; swung (quintuplet) hi-hat, slightly early snare.

“How to Play the Pandeiro for Capoeira.” Dende Arts. dendearts.com/blog/how-to-play-the-pandeiro-for-capoeira/. Thumb, fingertips, heel, fingertips.

“Latin Percussion Applications in the Jazz Band.” Jazz Education Network. jazzednet.org/resources/latin-percussion-applications-in-the-jazz-band/. Cha-cha-chá: bell in quarters, güiro long quarter + two eighths.

“Motown Groove.” Soundbrenner. www.soundbrenner.com/blogs/articles/motown-groove. Snare on 2 and 4 or on all four beats; tambourine in eighths; kick on 1 and 3.

“New jack swing.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_jack_swing. Offbeat-accented sixteenth-note triplets; the TR-808 snare; TR-808, LinnDrum, SP-1200.

“The Pandeiro.” Acoustics Today, July 2007, p. 41. acousticstoday.org/issues/2007AT/Jul2007/files/basic-html/page41.html. Pandeiro batida: thumb, fingertips, heel, fingertips.

“Salsa (musical structure).” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salsa_(musical_structure). Conga marcha (tumbao) and its alignment with clave; the timbale bell from the cáscara.

“Salsa Rhythm: How to Play Tumbao.” Salsa Vida. www.salsavida.com/?p=509. Open tones on 4 and 4&, the slap on 2.

“Timbale: Playing the Son.” Artdrum. www.artdrum.com/TIMBALE_PLAYING_THE_SON.HTM. Paila: left hand muffled on 2, open on 4; the tumbao is the cha-cha-chá conga part, faster.

“Trap music.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trap_music. About 140 bpm in half-time, deep 808 kicks with long decay, double- and triple-time hi-hats.

“Tumbao.” Soundbrenner. www.soundbrenner.com/blogs/articles/tumbao. Heel-toe, slap and open tones of the tumbao.

“Tumbao.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumbao. Cites Rebeca Mauleón, Salsa Guidebook.

Yamaha Corporation. MODX6+ / MODX7+ / MODX8+ Data List. Yamaha. usa.yamaha.com/files/download/other_assets/5/1583935/modx_plus_en_dl_a0.pdf. Drum Kit Assign List: the key of every sound in Pop Latin Kit, Real Brushes Kit, Jazz Brushes Kit and Brush Kit (kit-to-table match read from the page layout).

For students

“Backbeat.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backbeat. The backbeat on 2 and 4; the delayed or late backbeat.
